Acids and Bases.intro: Acids and bases are fundamental in chemistry. The pH scale measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
Acids and Bases.mnemonic: For acid reactions: 'MASH Makes Salts and Hydrogen' — Metal + Acid → Salt + Hydrogen. 'HASH Makes Water' — Hydroxide + Acid → Salt + H₂O. 'CASH Makes Water and CO₂' — Carbonate + Acid → Salt + H₂O + CO₂. For salt names: HCl → cHLoride, H₂SO₄ → SULphate, HNO₃ → NiTrate.

sections.title: The pH Scale
sections.text: The pH scale measures the concentration of H⁺ ions in a solution. pH runs from 0 to 14; below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.
points: pH 0–6 = acidic — high concentration of H⁺ ions; lower pH = more acidic (more H⁺)
pH 7 = neutral — pure water; [H⁺] = [OH⁻]
pH 8–14 = alkaline — high concentration of OH⁻ ions; higher pH = more alkaline
Strong acid — fully ionises in solution (e.g. HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻); low pH at same concentration as weak acid
Weak acid — partially ionises (e.g. CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻); higher pH than strong acid at same concentration
Measuring pH — universal indicator (colour change), pH meter (most accurate), litmus (rough)

sections.title: Reactions of Acids
sections.text: Acids react with metals, metal oxides, metal hydroxides, and metal carbonates in characteristic ways, always forming a salt.
points: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas (e.g. 2HCl + Mg → MgCl₂ + H₂)
Acid + metal oxide → salt + water (e.g. H₂SO₄ + CuO → CuSO₄ + H₂O)
Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water (neutralisation, e.g. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O)
Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (e.g. 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂)
Test for hydrogen — lit splint gives squeaky pop
Test for CO₂ — turns limewater milky

sections.title: Strong vs Weak Acids and Naming Salts
sections.text: Acid strength (strong/weak) is different from acid concentration (concentrated/dilute). Salts are named from the acid and base used.
points: Strong acid — 100% ionised in water: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃
Weak acid — partially ionised (equilibrium): ethanoic acid, citric acid, carbonic acid
Strength ≠ concentration — a weak acid can be concentrated; a strong acid can be dilute
HCl → chloride salts: e.g. sodium chloride (NaCl)
H₂SO₄ → sulfate salts: e.g. copper sulfate (CuSO₄)
HNO₃ → nitrate salts: e.g. potassium nitrate (KNO₃)

keyTerms.def: A substance that produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution; pH below 7
A soluble base that produces OH⁻ ions in solution; pH above 7
A substance that neutralises an acid — includes metal oxides, hydroxides, and carbonates
The reaction between an acid and a base to form salt and water; H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
An ionic compound formed when the H⁺ in an acid is replaced by a metal ion
An acid that fully ionises in water — e.g. HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃
An acid that only partially ionises in water — e.g. ethanoic acid, citric acid

examTips: Neutralisation ionic equation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) — this is worth knowing for higher tier.
The name of the salt depends on the acid: HCl → chloride, H₂SO₄ → sulfate, HNO₃ → nitrate — learn these three.
Acid + carbonate reaction produces CO₂ as well as salt and water — don't forget the CO₂.
Strong acid strength is about degree of ionisation, NOT concentration — a dilute strong acid is still a strong acid.
commonMistakes: Confusing acid + carbonate (produces CO₂) with acid + metal oxide (no CO₂, only salt + water).
Confusing acid strength (strong/weak = degree of ionisation) with concentration (concentrated/dilute = amount dissolved).
Forgetting to include CO₂ in the products of acid + carbonate reactions.
clozePassages: Acids are substances that produce hydrogen ions (H⁺) in aqueous solution. Bases are substances that neutralise acids. An alkali is a soluble base that produces hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in solution. The pH scale runs from 0-14 — below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline. Universal indicator changes colour to show pH. Strong acids are fully ionised; weak acids are only partially ionised.

Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water. The general equation is: acid + base → salt + water. The salt formed depends on the acid and base used. Hydrochloric acid forms chloride salts, sulphuric acid forms sulphate salts, and nitric acid forms nitrate salts. The reaction between an acid and a metal carbonate also produces carbon dioxide gas.

Strong acids such as hydrochloric, sulphuric, and nitric acid are completely ionised in solution. Weak acids such as ethanoic acid and citric acid are only partially ionised. A solution of a weak acid at the same concentration as a strong acid has a higher pH. The strength of an acid is different from its concentration — a concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong acid, but it is still a weak acid.

Salts.intro: Salts are ionic compounds formed from neutralisation reactions. Making pure dry salt requires specific practical techniques.
Salts.mnemonic: For making salts remember: 'Excess, Filter, Evaporate' — EFE. Add EXCESS solid base/metal/carbonate (to ensure all acid reacts), FILTER off the excess solid, then EVAPORATE to crystallise the salt. For insoluble salts: just MIX two solutions (precipitation).

sections.title: Making Soluble Salts
sections.text: Soluble salts are made by reacting an acid with an excess of a base, metal, or carbonate. The excess solid is filtered off and the solution evaporated.
points: Step 1 — add excess solid base/carbonate/metal to the acid; ensures all the acid reacts
Step 2 — filter to remove the excess unreacted solid
Step 3 — evaporate the filtrate (solution) to concentrate it; allow to cool and crystallise
Step 4 — filter and dry the salt crystals
Why excess? — ensures all acid is neutralised; makes filtration effective to remove excess solid
Example — copper sulfate from CuO + H₂SO₄: add excess CuO to warm H₂SO₄; filter off excess CuO; evaporate blue solution

sections.title: Naming Salts
sections.text: The name of a salt comes from the metal in the base and the acid used. The acid provides the anion name.
points: Two-part name — metal name from the base + anion name from the acid
HCl → chloride: e.g. NaOH + HCl → NaCl (sodium chloride)
H₂SO₄ → sulfate: e.g. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ (copper sulfate)
HNO₃ → nitrate: e.g. KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ (potassium nitrate)
H₃PO₄ → phosphate: e.g. Ca(OH)₂ + H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ (calcium phosphate)

sections.title: Making Insoluble Salts by Precipitation
sections.text: Insoluble salts cannot be made by dissolving — they are made by mixing two solutions that contain the required ions, causing the insoluble salt to precipitate.
points: Precipitation — mixing two solutions to form an insoluble solid (precipitate)
Example — barium sulfate: BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
Method — mix solutions, filter off precipitate, wash with distilled water, dry
Ionic equation — Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) — spectator ions not included
Applications — water treatment (removing unwanted ions); testing for sulfate ions (barium chloride test)
Solubility rules — most chlorides, sulfates, nitrates are soluble; most carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble

keyTerms.def: The process of forming salt crystals from a saturated solution by evaporation and cooling
The formation of an insoluble solid (precipitate) from two solutions mixed together
The reaction of an acid with a base to form salt and water
Separation technique to remove insoluble solids from a liquid using filter paper
Ions present in solution that do not take part in the reaction — not included in ionic equations
More than the amount needed to react completely — ensures all of the other reactant is used up

examTips: For making soluble salts: always add EXCESS base to ensure all acid reacts, then FILTER off excess solid — examiners expect both steps.
For precipitation: state that an insoluble precipitate forms when two solutions are mixed; identify the correct ions.
Ionic equations for precipitation: only include the ions that react — leave out spectator ions (e.g. Na⁺, K⁺, NO₃⁻).
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add EXCESS base when making a soluble salt — without excess, some acid remains in the filtrate.
Trying to make an insoluble salt by the 'excess solid' method — insoluble salts must be made by precipitation.
Including spectator ions in ionic equations — only the reacting ions and precipitate should appear.
clozePassages: Salts are ionic compounds formed when an acid reacts with a base, metal, or carbonate. They can be made by reacting an acid with a metal (producing hydrogen gas), a metal oxide, a metal hydroxide, or a metal carbonate. The method chosen depends on whether the salt is soluble or insoluble. Insoluble salts are made by precipitation — mixing two solutions to form an insoluble product.

The name of a salt has two parts: the metal name from the base, and the acid name ending — chloride from hydrochloric acid, sulphate from sulphuric acid, nitrate from nitric acid. For example, copper sulphate is made from copper oxide and sulphuric acid. Excess copper oxide is added to ensure all the acid reacts. The excess solid is filtered off and the solution is evaporated to obtain crystals of the salt.

Precipitation reactions are used to make insoluble salts. Two solutions containing the required ions are mixed, and the insoluble salt forms as a precipitate. For example, barium sulphate can be made by mixing barium chloride solution with sodium sulphate solution. The precipitate is filtered, washed with distilled water, and dried. Precipitation is also used to remove unwanted ions from water in water treatment.

Reactivity Series.intro: The reactivity series ranks metals from most to least reactive. It can be used to predict displacement reactions and the stability of metal compounds.
Reactivity Series.mnemonic: Learn the reactivity series with: 'Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra In Loose Clothing, Silly Gold' — Potassium, Sodium, Calcium, Magnesium, Aluminium, Zinc, Iron, Lead, Copper, Silver, Gold. Most reactive at the top, least at the bottom.

sections.title: The Reactivity Series
sections.text: The reactivity series ranks metals in order of how readily they lose electrons and react with water, acids, and oxygen.
points: Most reactive — K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au (least reactive)
Most reactive metals — react vigorously with cold water and acids; form very stable oxides
Middle metals — react with acids but slowly or not with cold water (e.g. iron rusts slowly)
Least reactive metals — copper, silver, gold do not react with dilute acids; found native (uncombined) in Earth's crust
Hydrogen is included — metals above hydrogen in the series displace it from acids
Extraction method — metals above carbon extracted by electrolysis; below carbon extracted by reduction with carbon

sections.title: Displacement Reactions
sections.text: A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. The more reactive metal gets oxidised while the less reactive one is reduced.
points: Rule — more reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its compound
Example — Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu (zinc displaces copper; zinc more reactive)
Observations — the solid copper deposits on zinc; blue colour fades (Cu²⁺ removed); zinc dissolves
Example 2 — Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (iron is more reactive than copper)
Cannot happen in reverse — Cu + ZnSO₄ → no reaction (copper less reactive than zinc)
Ionic half equations — Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction)

sections.title: Metal Extraction and the Reactivity Series
sections.text: The method used to extract a metal from its ore depends on its position in the reactivity series.
points: Very reactive metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) — too reactive to be reduced by carbon; extracted by electrolysis
Middle reactivity metals (Zn, Fe, Pb) — extracted by reduction with carbon (coke) in a blast furnace
Iron extraction — Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (carbon monoxide reduces the iron oxide)
Aluminium extraction — electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃ dissolved in cryolite); expensive
Low reactivity metals (Cu, Ag, Au) — found native or easily extracted; copper also obtained by displacement
Bioleaching and phytomining — newer sustainable methods for extracting copper from low-grade ores

keyTerms.def: A list of metals arranged in order of decreasing reactivity, from potassium (most) to gold (least)
A reaction where a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt
A metal found uncombined in the Earth's crust — e.g. gold and silver; found because they are unreactive
In metal extraction, the removal of oxygen from a metal oxide — done using carbon or carbon monoxide
Process of using electrical energy to extract very reactive metals that cannot be reduced by carbon
Using bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores — a sustainable extraction method

examTips: Only a MORE reactive metal can displace a LESS reactive one — never the other way around; state this principle clearly.
Remember the extraction method links to reactivity: very reactive (above carbon) → electrolysis; less reactive (below carbon) → reduction with carbon/CO.
In displacement reactions, identify which metal is oxidised (loses electrons, forms ions) and which is reduced (gains electrons, forms atoms).
commonMistakes: Saying a less reactive metal can displace a more reactive one — this CANNOT happen.
Forgetting that aluminium is extracted by electrolysis despite being common — it is very reactive, above carbon in the series.
Not explaining displacement in terms of electron transfer — always link to oxidation (metal loses electrons) and reduction (ion gains electrons).
clozePassages: The reactivity series ranks metals in order of their reactivity. The most reactive metals are at the top (e.g. potassium, sodium, calcium) and the least reactive at the bottom (e.g. gold, platinum). More reactive metals react more vigorously with water, acids, and oxygen. A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compound. The reactivity series is used to predict reactions and determine extraction methods.

Displacement reactions occur when a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. For example, zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate solution: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. The zinc is oxidised (loses electrons) and the copper ions are reduced (gain electrons). Displacement reactions demonstrate the relative positions of metals in the reactivity series.

Metals high in the reactivity series are harder to extract from their ores because they form very stable compounds. Potassium, sodium, calcium, and aluminium are extracted by electrolysis. Metals in the middle of the series, such as iron, are extracted by reduction with carbon in a blast furnace. Metals low in the reactivity series, such as gold and silver, are often found as native metals and are easy to extract.

Redox.intro: Redox reactions involve the simultaneous transfer of electrons. Oxidation and reduction always occur together.
Redox.mnemonic: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Never forget this! Also: 'LEO the lion says GER' — Lose Electrons = Oxidation; Gain Electrons = Reduction. The reducing AGENT gets oxidised; the oxidising AGENT gets reduced — they are agents DOING the work to the other substance.

sections.title: OIL RIG
sections.text: OIL RIG is the essential memory aid for redox: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons. Both always happen simultaneously.
points: Oxidation — loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen); oxidation number INCREASES
Reduction — gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen); oxidation number DECREASES
Redox reaction — oxidation and reduction always occur simultaneously; electrons are transferred
Reducing agent — the substance that donates electrons to another; it is itself OXIDISED
Oxidising agent — the substance that accepts electrons; it is itself REDUCED
Example — Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu: Zn is oxidised (loses 2e⁻); Cu²⁺ is reduced (gains 2e⁻)

callout.label: Memory Aid
callout.text: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons)

sections.title: Oxidation States
sections.text: Oxidation states (numbers) track electron transfer in redox reactions. An increase in oxidation state = oxidation; a decrease = reduction.
points: Oxidation state rules — uncombined element = 0; O usually −2; H usually +1; sum of states in neutral compound = 0
Increase in oxidation state = oxidised (lost electrons)
Decrease in oxidation state = reduced (gained electrons)
Example — Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂: Fe goes from +3 to 0 (reduced); C in CO goes from +2 to +4 (oxidised)
Half equations — Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction)
Electrons cancel — in a balanced redox equation, electrons lost = electrons gained

sections.title: Redox in Familiar Reactions
sections.text: Many familiar chemical processes are redox reactions — combustion, rusting, metal extraction, and electrolysis all involve electron transfer.
points: Combustion — C + O₂ → CO₂: carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen / loses electrons)
Rusting — iron is oxidised: 4Fe + 3O₂ + water → 2Fe₂O₃ (iron gains oxygen, increases oxidation state)
Displacement reactions — more reactive metal is oxidised; less reactive metal ion is reduced
Electrolysis — at cathode: reduction (ions gain electrons); at anode: oxidation (ions lose electrons)
Metal extraction by carbon — metal oxide is reduced (loses O); carbon is oxidised (gains O)

keyTerms.def: Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen); oxidation state increases
Gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen); oxidation state decreases
A reaction involving simultaneous oxidation and reduction; electrons are transferred
Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons); Reduction Is Gain (of electrons) — the key mnemonic
A substance that donates electrons to another substance — it is itself oxidised
A substance that accepts electrons from another substance — it is itself reduced
A number representing the degree of oxidation of an atom — increases when oxidised, decreases when reduced

examTips: OIL RIG — memorise and use it every time: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain.
The reducing AGENT is OXIDISED (it donates electrons); the oxidising AGENT is REDUCED (it accepts electrons) — these seem counterintuitive but follow from OIL RIG.
In half equations, check electrons are balanced: same number lost on oxidation half equation as gained on reduction half equation.
commonMistakes: Confusing which species is oxidised and which is reduced — apply OIL RIG systematically to each species.
Saying the oxidising agent is oxidised — the oxidising agent is REDUCED (it gains electrons and does the oxidising of the other substance).
Forgetting that oxidation and reduction ALWAYS occur simultaneously — you cannot have one without the other.
clozePassages: Oxidation is the loss of electrons. Reduction is the gain of electrons. These always occur simultaneously in a redox reaction. The acronym OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain) is a useful memory aid. The substance that loses electrons is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent. The substance that gains electrons is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

In terms of oxygen, oxidation is the gain of oxygen and reduction is the loss of oxygen. When iron rusts, it is oxidised by oxygen and water. When iron oxide is reduced in a blast furnace using carbon monoxide, the iron oxide loses oxygen. Both definitions — in terms of oxygen and in terms of electrons — are consistent and give the same result. The electron transfer definition is more widely applicable.

Oxidation states can be used to track electron transfer in redox reactions. Hydrogen has an oxidation state of +1 in compounds and oxygen has an oxidation state of -2 in most compounds. If the oxidation state of an element increases, it has been oxidised. If it decreases, it has been reduced. Assigning oxidation states helps identify which species are oxidised and which are reduced in complex reactions.

Electrolysis.intro: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to break down ionic compounds. It is used to extract reactive metals and purify copper.
Electrolysis.mnemonic: Remember: 'Cats Are Negative, An-odes Are Positive' (Cathode = negative = reduction; Anode = positive = oxidation). Or: 'CAtions go to CAthode; ANions go to ANode' — both start with the same letters! PANIC: Positive Anode Negative Is Cathode.

sections.title: How Electrolysis Works
sections.text: Electrolysis uses direct current to decompose an ionic compound. The compound must be molten or dissolved so that ions are free to move.
points: Electrolyte — molten or dissolved ionic compound; ions must be free to move
Cathode (negative electrode) — positive ions (cations) attracted here; they GAIN electrons → REDUCED
Anode (positive electrode) — negative ions (anions) attracted here; they LOSE electrons → OXIDISED
At cathode — metal deposited OR hydrogen gas produced (if metal is above hydrogen in reactivity series)
At anode — oxygen gas produced (from OH⁻ or water) OR halogen gas (if halide ion present — halide preferentially discharged)
OIL RIG applies — cathode = reduction (gain electrons); anode = oxidation (lose electrons)

sections.title: Products from Electrolysis
sections.text: The products of electrolysis depend on what is being electrolysed. Key examples include molten ionic compounds, brine, and copper sulfate solution.
points: Molten ionic compound — cathode: metal atom deposited; anode: non-metal gas produced (e.g. molten NaCl → Na at cathode, Cl₂ at anode)
Brine (NaCl solution) — cathode: H₂ gas; anode: Cl₂ gas; remaining: NaOH solution
Copper sulfate solution — cathode: Cu deposited; anode: O₂ gas (or Cu dissolved if copper anode — used in purification)
Aluminium extraction — electrolysis of molten Al₂O₃ (dissolved in molten cryolite to lower MP); Al at cathode, O₂ at anode
Products of brine electrolysis — H₂ (used to make margarine/fuel cells), Cl₂ (bleach, PVC), NaOH (soap, paper)

sections.title: Half Equations at Electrodes
sections.text: Half equations describe what happens at each electrode — showing electrons gained or lost.
points: Cathode (reduction) — add electrons to the left side: e.g. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
Anode (oxidation) — electrons on the right side: e.g. 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; or 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻
Hydrogen at cathode — 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (or 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻)
Balancing half equations — balance atoms first, then balance charge by adding electrons
Overall equation — add half equations together (electrons must cancel) to get full balanced equation

keyTerms.def: Decomposition of an ionic compound using electrical energy
The negative electrode — where reduction occurs; cations are discharged here
The positive electrode — where oxidation occurs; anions are discharged here
The molten or dissolved ionic compound through which current passes during electrolysis
Concentrated sodium chloride solution — electrolysed to produce Cl₂, H₂, and NaOH
An equation showing what happens at one electrode, including electrons gained or lost
A mineral (Na₃AlF₆) used to dissolve aluminium oxide and lower its melting point in aluminium extraction

examTips: Cathode = NEGATIVE = REDUCTION (cations discharged, gain electrons). Anode = POSITIVE = OXIDATION (anions discharged, lose electrons).
When electrolysing a solution: hydrogen forms at the cathode instead of the metal if the metal is MORE reactive than hydrogen.
At the anode in solutions: halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) are preferentially discharged over OH⁻ — so Cl₂ forms instead of O₂ if chloride is present.
commonMistakes: Confusing anode (positive, oxidation) and cathode (negative, reduction) — use the PANIC mnemonic: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.
Saying metals always form at the cathode in aqueous solution — if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, H₂ forms instead.
Forgetting the three useful products of brine electrolysis — hydrogen, chlorine, AND sodium hydroxide.
clozePassages: Electrolysis uses an electric current to decompose an ionic compound. The compound must be molten or dissolved in water so that its ions are free to move. Positive ions (cations) move to the negative electrode (cathode) where they gain electrons and are reduced. Negative ions (anions) move to the positive electrode (anode) where they lose electrons and are oxidised.

The electrolysis of brine (sodium chloride solution) produces three useful products: chlorine gas at the anode, hydrogen gas at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide solution. These are used to make bleach, plastics (PVC), and margarine. The electrolysis of aluminium oxide extracts aluminium metal, which is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon. Aluminium smelting requires large amounts of electrical energy.

When electrolysing a solution, the products depend on which ions are present and their relative discharge positions. At the cathode, hydrogen is produced if the metal ion is more reactive than hydrogen. At the anode, oxygen is produced unless a halide ion is present — halides are preferentially discharged. Electroplating uses electrolysis to coat one metal with another, improving appearance or resistance to corrosion.
